examples.solution_text:
No edge is directed into $K$, so $K$ is the source.
No edge is directed out of $N$, so $N$ is the sink.
Use the arrows, not the positions of the vertices.

At most $23$ L/min can travel from $S$ to $A$.
The arrow allows that direction only.
The $23$ is a capacity, not an actual flow.

Every path from $S$ to $T$ starts with $SA$, $SB$ or $ST$.
The dashed line crosses all three edges.
No path from the source to the sink avoids the line.
The line completely separates the source from the sink, so it is a cut.

The source is $S$ and the sink is $T$.
The line crosses $SE$, $EB$ and $BC$.
Every path from $S$ to $T$ uses $SE$ or $BC$, so every path crosses the line.
The direction of $EB$ does not leave a path that avoids the line.
The source and sink are completely separated, so the line is a cut.

(a) Every path from $S$ to $T$ uses $AT$ or $BT$. The line crosses both edges, so it completely separates source and sink. It is a cut.
(b) The line crosses $AT$, but the path $S \rightarrow B \rightarrow T$ avoids it. The source and sink are not completely separated, so it is not a cut.

The line crosses $AC$ and $AD$.
The path $S \rightarrow B \rightarrow D \rightarrow T$ avoids the line.
Crossing several edges is not enough: a cut must completely separate the source from the sink.
The dashed line is not a cut.

methods.description: Identify the source and sink from arrow directions rather than vertex positions.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/Network Flow.md lines 58–64, Flow Network

methods.description: Interpret an edge capacity as a maximum movement rate in the arrow direction, rather than actual flow.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/Network Flow.md lines 64–80, Flow Network and Maximum Flow

methods.description: Explain a valid cut by showing that every directed source-to-sink path crosses the line; this applies at the source, sink or between intermediate vertices.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/Network Flow.md lines 268–277 and 302–304, Cuts

methods.description: Explain that a crossing edge directed back towards the source side does not invalidate complete source-to-sink separation.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/Network Flow.md lines 283–288 and 296–308, Cuts and Calculate cut capacity example

methods.description: Disprove cut validity by tracing a directed source-to-sink path that avoids the line. Additional bypass paths use the same method.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/Network Flow.md lines 271–277 and Development question 7(b), lines 477–488

methods.description: Apply the complete-separation test to each candidate line, explaining validity through crossed paths and invalidity through an avoiding path.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 6 Standard/Network Flow.md lines 271–277, Cut / Not a cut comparison

existingExamples.reason: Correct source/sink identification with a useful reversed orientation. Editable diagram contains the necessary arrows and givens without answer annotations. Plain solution prose inherits renderer blue; no continuation equations require gutters.

Correctly distinguishes directed capacity from actual flow and retains units. Diagram supplies only givens. Plain solution prose and inline mathematics inherit renderer blue; no continuation gutter is needed.

The line crosses all three source edges, supporting the complete-separation explanation. Diagram and solution are adequate without additional annotations. Solution inherits renderer blue and contains no relation-led working.

The curved line crosses SE, EB and BC and separates source from sink. The reverse-edge explanation follows the supplied teaching without introducing cut-capacity calculations. Editable prose inherits renderer blue; no equation gutter or answer diagram is required.

The complete line crosses both sink edges; the partial line leaves the lower path open. The paired diagrams support comparing candidate lines. Solutions inherit renderer blue, retain ordinary black diagrams and require no continuation gutters.

The partial line crosses AC and AD while leaving S-B-D-T open. The explanation addresses the stated misconception using the taught bypass method. Plain prose inherits renderer blue; no equation gutter or derived diagram annotation is needed.
